nameStory: This moth gets its name from two key features: its distinctive reddish-brown head that stands out against its pale wings, and its caterpillar stage, which moves like a classic "inchworm" or measuring worm. The larvae arch their backs and seem to measure the ground as they crawl, giving the whole moth family the nickname "geometers" meaning "earth measurers" in Greek.
description: The Red-headed Inchworm Moth is a small, delicate moth with wings that span about an inch across. Its most striking feature is the reddish-brown head that contrasts with wings colored in soft tones ranging from milky tan to gray-brown. The wings are marked with distinctive dark brown spots and lines that create a subtle but recognizable pattern. Like other geometer moths, it holds its wings horizontally when at rest, creating a triangular silhouette.

idTips.label: Reddish-brown head
idTips.description: The head has a warm, rusty-brown color that looks almost copper-tinted in good light, contrasting noticeably with the paler wing colors

idTips.label: Dark coastal spots
idTips.description: Look for 3-4 distinct dark brown marks along the leading edge of each forewing, creating a dotted pattern that feels rough to gentle touch

idTips.label: Rectangular wing spot
idTips.description: A larger, almost square-shaped dark spot sits prominently near the wing tip, looking like a small brown window pane

idTips.label: Wing color variation
idTips.description: Overall wing color ranges from creamy, milk-like tan to deeper gray-brown, with a soft, powdery texture typical of moth scales

idTips.label: Horizontal wing position
idTips.description: When resting, holds wings spread horizontally rather than folded vertically, creating a flat, triangular outline about an inch wide

habitat: Look for Red-headed Inchworm Moths in pine forests and mixed woodlands throughout New England, especially where Eastern White Pine grows abundantly. They're drawn to areas with mature pines, as their caterpillars feed almost exclusively on pine needles. You'll often spot them near outdoor lights at night or resting on tree trunks and wooden surfaces during the day.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, often found resting on pine bark during warm afternoons or attracted to porch lights on mild evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season runs through July and August, when they're most active and easiest to spot around lights or during evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Adult flight activity winds down by early fall, though occasional stragglers may appear on warm September nights.
seasonality.winter: Overwintering as pupae in the soil or leaf litter beneath pine trees, completely absent as adults during cold months.

funFact: The caterpillars of this moth are pine needle specialists that can actually change the chemical composition of their body to match the defensive compounds found in their host trees, essentially becoming "living pine needles" that taste terrible to birds and other predators.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Psamatodes abydata, but that species lacks the telltale dark brown spots along the wing's leading edge - remember "Red-headed moths have roadside markers" referring to those distinctive coastal spots that line up like highway signs.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an "inchworm moth," the adult doesn't move like an inchworm at all - only the caterpillar does. The name refers to the larval stage's distinctive looping movement, which occurs because geometer moth caterpillars lack the middle pairs of legs that other caterpillars use for walking.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Lesser Maple Spanworm Moth in the same genus, the Red-headed Inchworm Moth has that distinctive reddish-brown head coloring and feeds exclusively on pines rather than maples. The wing patterns are similar, but the Red-headed species has more pronounced dark spots along the wing's leading edge and tends to be found in coniferous rather than deciduous habitats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Red-headed Inchworm Moth, the Lesser Maple Spanworm has more subdued coloration without the distinctive reddish head coloring.
